The other evening when the committee rose we were discussing research work carried on in different cities regarding the purchase and consumption of agricultural products. I asked the minister whether any investigation had been made into the consumption of vegetable oils and the effect upon the sale of other agricultural products. The minister replied in the negative, and he was asked whether any such investigation was contemplated. I think it is desirable in the interest of agriculture, and particularly of the live stock industry, that some such investigation be made. Would the minister tell us who initiates these investigations? Under whose authority are they begun? Is it by his own authority, or has the department power to initiate them? If it is the minister's prerogative, will he consider the advisability of inquir-
ing into the effect of the increasing sale of vegetable oils in Canada in recent years upon the sale of animal fats for spreading and shortening purposes?

The investigation into the use of vegetable oils that has been asked by certain individuals is an investigation of the type that might be carried on by the tariff board. As I understand it the question which has been submitted to that board is whether or not the dairy industry should be given some protection through some action regarding the importation of vegetable oils. That is not a question that would be investigated by the economics branch of this department.

I scarcely agree with the minister. I was not asking an investigation into the merits of placing a tariff on vegetable oils or otherwise; but it is undoubtedly true that the sale of vegetable oils in Canada is increasing very rapidly, and naturally it must have some effect upon the sale of animal fats and oils. I think it might very well come within the scope of any investigation to determine to what extent these vegetable oils are displacing animal fats for spreading and shortening purposes. I do not wish to carry the matter further than to say that I believe it would be in the interests of agriculture generally if the minister would initiate such an investigation.
While I am on my feet I should like to ask the minister one further question. The other day he made some reference to the fact that a study was being made of the cost of farm living. I wonder how far that investigation has been carried and how it is being conducted. Is it being carried on in all parts of the dominion or only in Ontario or some other provinces?

Most of these investigations are earned on in cooperation with the provincial authorities and, in some instances, agricultural colleges and universities. They are of a local nature in the sense that at one time they may be carried on in Alberta, at another time in Ontario and at another time in Nova Scotia, but there is a relationship between the investigations in one part and those in others.

Reverting for a moment to
the question of vegetable oils, perhaps the Minister of Finance could tell us whether or not there has been an investigation made by the tariff board. I was under the impression that he ordered an investigation by that board into the importation of vegetable oils,

which arose, so far as my interest in it was concerned, not only as regards the dairying interests in my district but also in connection with the competition it afforded to fish oils made from the reduction of pilchards on the Pacific coast. Perhaps my memory is bad, but I gathered that the matter was being investigated by the tariff board. Has the Minister of Finance any knowledge of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) is quite correct, Mr. Chairman. The reference to the tariff board of the matter of tariffs on vegetable oils and matters connected therewith was made some time ago. I cannot recollect the date, but in any event it was within the past year Hearings have taken place; submissions have been made, and there has been very considerable argument about the whole matter. Offhand I cannot state the stage of the proceedings at the moment, but a very thorough inquiry is proceeding.

I realize
that it is difficult to discuss a matter that is now before the tariff board; but on the other hand, as the hon member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) has stated, the situation warrants further investigation by the department into the effect on our agricultural products of the importation of vegetable oils. I presume if it is impossible to discuss the matter under thP item it may be impossible to discuss it under any other. The government may later consider any recommendations that may be made by the tariff board in regard to the tariff on vegetable oils, but I think if investigation discloses that vegetable oils am replacing animal fats and oils to a considerable extent there may be some other method of assisting and protecting the producers of animal fats in this country. The tariff board is dealing with the tariff phase of the issue; nevertheless I think under this item the government might well institute investigations to ascertain to what extent animal fats and oils are being replaced by the vegetable oils that are shipped into this country. The government should consider that matter very carefully, as a government; and it is the responsibility of the Department of Agriculture to consider the effect on agriculture in this country. I am not so much concerned with the manner in which the government might assist the farmers, whether by implementing any recommendations made by the tariff board or by the imposition of a processing tax, but I do feel that this question deeply affects agriculture, and might well be considered by this economics branch instead of being left entirely to the tariff board as a tariff or fiscal matter.
Personally I think the importation of these vegetable oils affects the very basis of the agricultural industry in this dominion. I know of nothing that promises so adversely to affect Canadian agriculture as the importation of substitutes for animal fats and animal oils. The live stock industry is recognized by all outstanding agriculturists, both in the department and in various parts of the dominion, as one of the most important branches of agriculture. If we are to perpetuate a sound agricultural industry in Canada we must maintain a prosperous live stock industry. I think every farmer within the sound of my voice will agree with that general principle, and that industry is being threatened by the greatly increased importation of vegetable oils and the ever-widening use of these oils as shortening, replacing lard. It is possible that in the not far distant future they may be used in the manufacture of substitutes for butter and other dairy products. When one realizes that to-day we find it necessary to export more than half the lard production in Canada one realizes the effect of these importations on our live stock industry, and there is no doubt that the almost prohibitive tariff against the importation of vegetable oils into the United States has had the effect of increasing the importations into this country. I do not mean to say that the imposition of tariffs is the only method of relieving the situation. While we are speaking about agricultural economics I must observe that I know of no single factor which affects so adversely the agricultural situation throughout Canada as does this great increase in importations of what might be described as a substitute for live stock products. It may be said that these many millions of pounds of imported vegetable oils are inedible. While that may be true it is also true that much of the oil imported as inedible is made edible before it reaches the Canadian market.
I believe the department would do well to consider means of relieving the situation, and as the Minister of Agriculture is the one most responsible to agriculture in Canada I suggest that he recommend to the government effective measures through which this serious situation may be remedied. In making these observations I believe I am not speaking out of turn, although the Minister of Finance has declared that the subject is before the tariff board. It seems to me that some form of taxation would be highly justified, in view of the fact that these importations strike at the very roots of successful agriculture and would have the effect of destroying our live stock industry.

I have received about five hundred letters from daily farmers in the northern section of Alberta, and especially from my own constituency, dealing with the problem of the importation of vegetable oil. I have no doubt other hon. members have received similar letters. In order that hon. members may be familiar with the situation I should like to read one letter.
Is the hon. member referring to letters or only to circulars which came through the mail?
They are circular statements signed by individual farmers.
But they are not letters.
They are letters in the respect I have indicated.
If they are signed by individual farmers they are letters.
And they are signed by individual farmers.
Handed to them to sign.	.
Signed by individual farmers who object to large importations of vegetable oil.
Propaganda.

Propaganda it may be, from your standpoint; but at the same time the dairy industry in Alberta and in other provinces must be protected. I am not saying it will have to be protected by the imposition of high tariffs upon vegetable oils, but there should be some way of helping the dairy farmers. The letter is as follows:
Dear Sir,-
I note that last year there were over 200,000,000 pounds of vegetable oils imported into Canada, chiefly from tropical countries, practically duty free, and that the quantity of shortening manufactured in Canada, not made from animal fat, has doubled since 1932. I have every reason to believe that the substitution of cheap foreign vegetable oils for Canadian produced animal fats is becoming a serious menace to Canada's 750,000 farmers.
Something must be done about this menace, for we farmers can't compete with the cheap native labour of the tropics. I urge you, therefore, to take such steps as will cause a duty to be placed on these imported vegetable oils as outlined in the application of the National Dairy Council to the tariff board in December, 1936. Successful diversified farming can only be continued through the encouragement of the live stock and dairy industries. As one of your constituents, depending on mixed farming for a living, I urge you to support a reasonable and fair tariff on the importation of these foreign substitutes for Canadian produced animal fats.
[Mr w. E. Rnwo.l
We know that very large areas of Canada are dependent upon the dairy industry. If the industry is not aided by the federal government the substitution of vegetable oils will have serious effects.
How?
Use your head.
Some are not accustomed to using their heads.
You promised fifty-eent butter in 1930 and we got five-cent butter.

If large quantities of vegetable oils are brought into Canada and used as shortening in the baking industry we will lose the local market for products we can produce in great abundance. I would urge the Minister of Agriculture to put his experts on agricultural economic planning to work on the subject. They should see that the dairy industry of Canada is properly protected.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak because of the pleas put forward in the last few moments. Although I represent a city constituency, I come from an agricultural province. I believe the city, part of which I represent, knows as well as any city can know the needs and desires of farmers, and recognizes as perhaps no other city does how completely and fully its own prosperity is tied up with the prosperity of the surrounding farming community. I hope that the government will not be influenced by pleas of the sort which have just been made for the imposition of tariffs on these products. I do not know for certain that all the representatives from Manitoba are in agreement with me, but I believe they are. I have spoken with the Manitoba members on the subject and have heard no voice in favour of the tariff now sought. I did not wish the moment to pass without speaking, especially in view of the silence of several representatives from Saskatchewan, which might indicate an acquiescence.
I believe the people in western Canada realize that they cannot at one and the same time ask for a general lowering of tariffs and an increase in the tariff on these particular commodities. Taking it by and large, it will be found that the farming communities will be consistent in the requests they make from time to time. I am well aware a certain campaign has been put on in favour of a tariff increase in this connection, and that some sections of the farming communities may be in favour of it. However it is my belief it will be found that no representative of the great province of Manitoba-and cer-

Supply-Agriculture-Economics
tainly Manitoba is an agricultural province, with many dairy farmers-will be in favour of this particular plea.

I have listened with interest and attention to the observations of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Maybank). I do not know just what is the attitude of the farming population of Manitoba tow'ard this question, but I venture to say that many of them want something done to curb the importation and sale of vegetable oils which are being used in preference to animal fats produced in our own country. The hon. gentleman has referred to the attitude of agriculture generally regarding the tariff, but he will find that in certain parts of this country the farmers are not asking for lower tariffs. All that they ask is that they be placed in a position of equality with other industries throughout the dominion so far as the tariff is concerned.
The hon. gentleman has referred to the propaganda being carried on, but I know that if conditions were reversed, if other classes of goods were coming in to displace other Canadian products, a more intensive campaign of propaganda would be carried on. 1 have in my hand a clipping containing a statement made by the president of Canada Packers in which he states that if a certain amount of protection were granted to this industry it would mean a third of a cent per pound on every hog slaughtered and a fifth of a cent per pound on, every steer. If hen. members will take the trouble to estimate what that would return to the farmers of Canada they will realize that it would mean from $6,000,000 to S7.500.000 annually. That is a considerable item.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) did not say that he was putting forth an argument on behalf of the consumer. His argument was rather on the ground that they have consistently been asking for freer trade and in this instance they had to be consistent again. It seems to me that his argument is not at all well founded. I did not rise at this time to enter into a discussion of this matter. All I ask the minister to do is to authorize an investigation into the extent to which imported vegetable oils are displacing animal fats produced in Canada. It seems to me that that would come well within this vote. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has stated that the matter is being inquired into by the tariff board, but I doubt if that investigation would be as thorough as one which could be made by officials of the department
who would go to cities and towns and other parts of the country and make a house to house investigation.

The importation and
use of vegetable oils has a relationship not only to the dairy industry but also to the live stock industry. If vegetable oils replace anything, it is animal fats rather than the products of the dairy industry. The whole matter of the relationship of these different products has been referred to the tariff board. I do not think it would be proper for the economics branch of the Department of Agriculture to start a second inquiry when the matter is before the tariff board. However, everything that has been mentioned here will naturally be given consideration during this investigation.

The army of privilege fights hard and never dies. The men who have been making an argument to-day in favour of restriction are the men who opposed a reciprocity agreement with the United States which gave us access to the American market. We cannot continue to export unless we continue to import. In 1930 our exports to the United Kingdom were $283,000,000; in 1937 they were $409,000,000.
Give us the figures for 1928.

I will let my hon. friend choose any year he washes, but if I were to give those it would only show the extent to which our trade fell off after the government of my hon. friend came into office. I do not want to make this a political issue. The imports from the United Kingdom dropped from $1S9,000,000 to $129,000,000. There is a strong feeling in the United Kingdom that we drove a very hard bargain when we negotiated the empire agreements with that country. A bargain is never a real bargain unless both parties to the transaction make a profit. When you drive a bargain in which the loss is entirely upon the other side, then you have lost the deal. That is especially so when it is a national transaction. You may have sharp practices with an individual and get away with it, but a nation must be honest, it must be square in its dealings.
Is the hon. member insinuating that sharp practices were applied to the British delegates at the conference?

The leader of the government of that day was emphatic in the statement that he w'as going to bargain in a tight, hard way, there is no question about

that. Were it not for that fact, where did the phrase, "blast our way into the markets of the world" originate?
I ask my hon. friend either to make his reflections clear or to retract them.
I am making my reflections quite clear. We drove a hard, tight bargain.

If the hon. gentleman will allow me to interrupt, I should like to say that there was no hard, tight bargain driven. I was at every conference between the British and Canadian delegates. If we had given all that the British delegates demanded, it would have been such a hard bargain for this country that industry could hardly have survived.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think this discussion is taking in a rather wide field. I would request hon. members to confine their remarks to the item before the committee. We are now on item No. 7.

I am dealing with a question involving the importation of vegetable oils into Canada, and I propose to submit this argument. We are now engaged in negotiation not only with the empire but with the United States for the extension of our markets. I submit that it is perfectly appropriate for me to point out that restrictions upon imports into this country must necessarily restrict exports. I was illustrating this fact by stating that in 1930 our exports to the United Kingdom were $283,000,000 and in 1937 they had increased to $409,000,000. Our imports from the United Kingdom were $189,000,000 and they dropped to $129,000,000. What happened in connection with vegetable oils? In 1933 our imports of vegetable oils from the United Kingdom amounted to $1,005,000 and in 1937 they had increased to $6,288,000. I submit that here was one little ewe lamb that we managed to offer to Great Britain. We offered her a market in this country for certain types of vegetable oil, and she took advantage of that offer. When there is one item of a few million dollars that seems to stand out, hon. gentlemen on the Conservative side rise up with one voice and say, "Let us restrict the imports of this commodity." I ask, where are we going? Do we want markets or do we not want them?

We are endeavouring as best we can to expand our markets for agricultural products not only in the United States but in the United Kingdom. It is, I submit, the most vital issue in this country to-day.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Can he tell me the amount in value of vegetable oils produced in the United Kingdom in any recent year?
We are buying them from there.
I should like to know what is the amount in value produced. The quantity produced is infinitesimal.

We are purchasing these oils refined or partly refined from the United Kingdom, and this is the market so far as the United Kingdom is concerned. I might counter iby asking what products we ship abroad and what proportion is produced in Canada; but we cannot go into those details to-day. The broad fact is that we must receive payment for the products which we export or we cannot continue to export them, and in face of the fact that we are now engaged in trade negotiations we have the suggestion made in this House of Commons, by men who, I presume, are definitely interested in the welfare of agriculture, that we should announce increased restrictions on the import of vegetable oils from the United Kingdom and also duties upon agricultural products coming in from the United States-that is what it ultimately involves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order arising out of your ruling, now that my hon. friend has stated what might be called the other side, could we not get back to the real point before the committee?-which, as I understand it, is whether this parliament is prepared to have $120,000 expended on the study of agricultural economies. I think, sir, your ruling was quite correct, that the discussion should be confined to the purpose for which the money is to be voted. The question is not the importation of vegetable oils or the usual budget debate on tariffs, either high or low, free trade or protection, but whether it is a good thing and a sound thing that there should be an organization in the Department of Agriculture to make an intensive study of agricultural economics, and of course to produce reports and make them available to parliament. The ruling, I submit, should be adhered to, but I hesitate to interrupt my hon. friend because he was stating the other side.

As your ruling, Mr. Chairman, was broad, and as the subject matter is very broad, may I point out with regard to trade with the United Kingdom that one should consider not only production over there. That would be a great mistake and would show very deep ignorance, because it is well known that with regard to butter, for instance, speaking in a wide sense, in England the sales of butter exceed greatly the production of butter, and the same with a great many other commodities.

speechtext: Order. The hon. member is out of order. We are discussing item 7, and if the hon. member will turn to page 55 of the details of the estimates he will find that the item is made up entirely of salaries. I would ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to item 7.

Mr. Chairman, I desire to deal again with the point brought up a moment ago with regard to the importation of vegetable 'oils. The hon. member for Haldi-mand (Mr. Senn) suggested that the effect of the importation of vegetable oils would be
the addition of, I think it was, approximately 35 cents a hundred, to the price of hogs in the Dominion of Canada. He quoted from a document which he said was prepared by Canada Packers, and I suppose I may be permitted now to quote from the same document in respect to this important item:
A careful calculation indicates that the duty proposed would involve an increase in the cost of household necessities not less than $15,000,000 per year. This is equivalent to $7 per family. And the weight of it would fall principally on labour and farm families, which are the largest consumers of bread and soap.
I submit that when we consider the investigation of vegetable oils we ought to consider very carefully the reduction in the purchasing power of the Canadian people which would result from the addition of a total bill of $15,000,000 to what labour, the farmer, and the consumers of Canada generally would have to pay for two ordinary household necessities.
May I ask the minister what the duties of the senior agricultural economists will be?

The senior agricultural economist is Mr. Booth, who was appointed in 1929 for the purpose of making investigations into the economic side of agriculture. It is not his duty, as I pointed out on three or four occasions last Thursday afternoon, to make investigations into the relationship of the tariff to the exportation of goods from Canada or the importation of goods into Canada. That is the duty of the tariff board. His duty is to make investigations in, say, Saskatchewan as to the costs of producing certain commodities or as to the cost of operating farms under certain circumstances, or as to whether one tyipe of farming would be beneficial as against another type, and all subjects of that kind having to do either with the marketing or with the production of farm commodities.

Have these inquiries
been begun? Are they being conducted at the present time?

Quite a number of them have been carried on over a period of years. There have been investigations into the marketing of fruit and vegetables, such as a study of the marketing of fruit and vegetables in the city of Toronto, an investigation of the variations in price received for apples exported from Nova Scotia, an investigation of distribution costs of fruits and vegetables distributed by wholesalers and jobbers, wholesale fruit and vegetable distribution costs. There is a whole page of them.

The minister mentioned western Canada. What work is being done in this regard in the prairie provinces?
Land utilization surveys, 1937, and an economic land utilization classification in Saskatchewan.

With regard to the surveys for land utilization, the members of that staff are, I believe, highly qualified soil chemists. Is this the place to ask for information regarding the rates of salary paid to these men? I understood the minister to tell me last year that they were classified as graduate-labourers.
The proper place to discuss that would be under experimental farms, on the next page.
The minister spoke of land utilization. I thought this might get the discussion back to the item, as a matter of fact.

Under this item I see: two senior agricultural economists, two agricultural economists, two senior assistant agricultural economists, two assistant agricultural economists, and one junior agricultural economist. I suggest that the minister should be very careful about economists, and should have business men of his own type in the first place; even if they are economists on the side I would have no objection to it. But in certain departments we have too many doctors, and I have suggested already that we should see them in full regalia: we have too many doctors, we have a pest of doctors, and at times they are fake doctors.
What about the lawyers?

I do not mean doctors of medicine like my hon. friend from Lanark;
I mean fake doctors in sciences, and especially doctors in philosophy. I am afraid of these people because they are dreamers, they are not practical men. I should like to see all these economists of lower grade replaced by men of high standing who have experience in agriculture, men of the type of the minister and other good men I see here in the house. They would do much more for the farmer and the country than some of those who are now in the Department of Agriculture. That is all I have to say about it for the time being.

Under this division of the department has any investigation been made into fruit marketing and production and dairy production in British Columbia? I believe that these activities are supposed to be carried on in conjunction with the local officials. If so, what has been done?
We have had investigations into creamery management and into milk consumption in British Columbia, and at present there is being organized an investigation into the fruit industry of that province.
Can the minister tell me where these different economists are located at the present time?

All of the officials whose positions are listed on page 55 work from a central office in Ottawa, but they may be carrying on duties in British Columbia or Nova Scotia or Saskatchewan-as a matter of fact, in any part of Canada.
Do they ever leave their Ottawa offices and go out and see the land at all?
Oh, yes; they go out continuously from the Ottawa office. They make investigations in different parts of Canada.
Go out and take a peek at it once in a while; is that it?

To come back to the
question asked a moment ago by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), I have in my hand a report of the Department of Agriculture, and amongst the duties listed under the economics branch are the following:
. The research activities of this branch were continued during the past year. The special phases of research emphasized have been: A study _ of the cost of production of milk in Ontario; land utilization in Saskatchewan and Alberta. . . .
I believe the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made it clear that he was referring to land utilization in Saskatchewan and Alberta, so that under this particular heading I believe I shall be in order in making a few remarks concerning land utilization in those two provinces.
I know the minister believes that eventually the drought areas of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta will come back into their own. For many years past I have agitated along the line that these people, instead of being kept continuously on relief in the areas in which they live, would be in a much better position if definite steps were taken to establish them-those of them for whom there is no hope in the future-in other areas in the northern parts of our provinces where they would have at least some opportunity and hope of reestablishment. This economics branch could very well undertake. for example, the study of wooded soils and their management. It is a subject which

Supply-Agriculture-Economics
in my opinion comes definitely within the purview of this branch. I understand that some work of this kind has been carried on in the past by various provincial governments, but in order to get at the root of this problem the economics branch should undertake a survey along lines which would give reasonable hope that a solution shall be found where apparently no solution exists at the present time.
I have often spoken about the Peace River country. I happen to know that in that particular part of Canada there is a vast area which needs development, which could easily locate many thousands of settlers who have no hope of recovering their lost fortunes in the places where they are settled at the present time. Apparently it is impossible to foresee with any degree of accuracy just how long it would take to rehabilitate them under the uncertain conditions which they have to face. The point is this, that year after year we in this parliament are required to appropriate vast sums of money in order to relieve the situation in the drought area, and I believe that one permanent way to meet that condition would be to investigate those parts of Canada which are capable of agricultural development. Eventually these people would no doubt be better off., and the government would benefit financially-and so would the taxpayers of Canada-if they were provided with new locations in areas where drought is unknown.
I realize that drought may be the result of a man-made condition and eventually might afflict these places which it is proposed to develop. That is why I maintain that proper research work in the undeveloped wooded areas in the northern parts of our provinces would certainly afford information which at the present time is not possessed by the Department of Agriculture. I do not know what work has been done along that line, but I believe that in that direction lies at least a possibility of doing away with a large part' of the burden of assistance which we have been carrying. Furthermore I wish to point out exactly what it means from the standpoint of the original family itself. We find these people in various drought areas in Saskatchewan living on hope year after year, always hoping that perhaps the next year will be a 'better one. Yet what happens? Bitter disappointment, bitter failure; that is always the extent to which their hopes materialize. I am sure there are certain places in Canada where we could very well settle these people, make new homes for them, and free them from the conditions under the disadvantages of which they are now existing. As I have
said, sometimes drought is the result of development and the opening up of the land too quickly; therefore I believe valuable investigatory work could be done by the economics branch of the department. I look forward to the day when the greatest volume of production in the prairie provinces will come from the northern section.
Under this same heading I notice that the marketing of fresh fruits and vegetables in Toronto is one of the functions performed by the economics branch.
Not the marketing; they are making an inquiry into marketing.

I would like them also to make an inquiry into the marketing possibilities in the Peace River country. I have agitated up there for many years for a coast outlet so that we could secure fresh fruits grown in British Columbia, and I shall lose no occasion to point out that in the Peace River country there is a vast market for British Columbia fresh fruits. The population is close to 70,000, and I am continually receiving letters to the effect that if there were an outlet from the Peace River country to the British Columbia fruit districts they would find in that part of Alberta a large market for their fruit. There is a vast.internal market for our products, and it should be one of the functions of the economics branch to ascertain and make known the manner in which these markets may be secured, or how the people can use the products which we produce in abundance. I think this study should be extended beyond the city of Toronto, and if it is found that other areas in Canada are capable of absorbing products from other parts of the country, the method to be used in getting the product to the market should be studied by that branch. We do use some fruit in the Peace River district at the present time, but the freight rates are so 'high and the haul so long that the people cannot afford to buy the British Columbia product. Yet in a direct line British Columbia is very close to the Peace River country.
Coming back to my first point, I think the minister should seriously consider the possibility of reestablishing settlers from the drought area in areas which are known to be productive but are at present undeveloped. We have hundreds of thousands of acres of such land in the Peace River country, and I am sure some arrangement could be made between the dominion government and the province concerned to permit these people to establish themselves in the northern part of our provinces. I speak of northern Alberta because I know it best, but I feel sure the
Supply-Agriculture-Economics

same thing applies to northern Saskatchewan, where I believe there are thousands of acres of undeveloped land awaiting settlers. Just picture the situation: we keep these people year after year in the dried out country in southern Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, while we have at our doors vast areas of land capable of production. The result of transferring these people would be to give them a better hope in the future, and materially and permanently to lessen the amount of money required to maintain them in the drought area. A relocation of the farmers from the drought areas of western Canada in productive areas now unoccupied is a subject which offers the minister great opportunity for study and action. I should like to know whether he considers that such a survey might well be made by the economics branch of his department.

The money for carrying on such work as that to which the hon. member has just referred is voted in the supplementary estimates in connection with our rehabilitation program in the drought area. It is not part of the work carried on directly by the Department of Agriculture, but it is carried out through that department under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. We shall have opportunity of discussing that at length when we come to that vote.
Then what do the words "land utilization in Saskatchewan and Alberta" mean?

These investigations are general inquiries into land utilization in all parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta-that is, occupied land. It does not refer to soil conservation, which is dealt with through the experimental farms branch and the universities of the different provinces through their agricultural colleges. It is really centralized in our plant at Swift Current in connection with the experimental farm there. The work consists of examining into the nature of different soils, and is carried on continuously. It is financed partly by the provincial governments, partly by grants from the federal government, and, as far as Saskatchewan is concerned, partly by a fund which was set up following the operations of the wheat board during the war, about $250,000, the interest on which is expended each year in making a soil survey. The whole province is now mapped. If you are going there to farm you can examine a map in my office or in any other agriculture department office in Canada and select the kind of soil you desire. The mapping of the other provinces is being proceeded with.

Do I understand that this branch of economics has the painful duty of attempting to make the drought areas produce? If that is so, then the suggestion I have made is well worthy of consideration. It might be possible to consolidate these two divisions in order that their combined efforts might 'lead to some satisfactory result.
That is done now.
Well, does "land utilization" mean an attempt to revive the dried-out areas in which the people are at present living on relief?

It deals with land now occupied by persons who have perhaps been living there for forty or fifty years. The economics branch gets a complete record of what has happened on that farm, analyses it and compares it with what has happened on another farm on a different type of land. As a result we get a picture of conditions in the different communities. All the information this economics branch gathers in that kind of survey is available to those who are carrying out what may be called land utilization policies. As we get the people off certain types of land, as a result of what we have found out we put them on other types of land. But the actual expenditure on this work of moving people about or doing anything in connection with those areas is made under our supplementary vote and not this vote.
This work is purely statistical?
Yes.

I understand that in certain provinces the land in certain areas is being repossessed by the province. Would there be any assistance from this branch to enable the provinces to know what areas they should retake or repossess? I am sure the minister is just as familiar as I am, or more so, with the particular projects going on in the various provinces.
Yes. that work has been going on since 1935, and it is the information which has been gathered through that work that is being utilized in our present rehabilitation work.

I understood the minister to say that maps were available showing the classification of the soils in the different provinces. Is that work undertaken north of latitude 54 in Saskatchewan? Has the department started on that?
There is some work being done up there, but I doubt if it is mapped north of 54. There is some line drawn across the north end.
I was thinking of the Goodsoil area.
There has been considerable work done in the Goodsoil area. I am not sure that it is mapped, but all the settled part in the northern part is pretty well mapped.
The work is being continued up there? That is all I wanted to know.
Yes.
Is it possible to get detailed reports of these surveys?
Yes, the maps can be secured. They are for sale at the experimental farm, and I think they can be procured also at the university of Saskatchewan.
Is there a report as well?
Yes, there is an inscription on the bottom of the map from which anyone can ascertain the condition of the soil at any point.

I was pleased to hear the minister say that the investigation was being carried on in Saskatchewan under this branch of his department, with respect to land utilization. I suggest that if such work had been done twenty-five or thirty years ago that province would not be in .much of the difficulty with which it is faced to-day, because a great deal of it never would have been turned up to the sun by the plow but would have remained ranching country. I presume that after these reports are made the minister will carry on his work of trying to convert some of that land back to ranching country, and possibly it will be better utilized in that way.
I want to suggest that this department might well investigate the system employed in Saskatchewan in collecting cream. The creameries are established in large centres, and there is much waste under the system now employed. Several large trucking companies cover the same territory, which certainly must mean added cost. I suggest-and this has been mentioned to me by members of the dairymen's association-that zones be established for the collection of cream and routes laid out by someone in authority, in order to avoid the overlapping occasioned by the trucks covering the same territory. Certain members of the dairymen's association have represented to me that a considerable saving

Supply-Agriculture-Economics
could be effected if this were done. I should like the minister to make some investigation along that line.
I was interested to-day in listening to the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deach-man) making his usual address on free trade, which as usual fell on deaf ears. He said what we wanted was markets. That is true enough, but I want to see the agriculturists and dairymen of western Canada have a fair opportunity to compete for at least their own domestic market. While this importation of vegetable oils continues I do not think they have a fair opportunity even to retain their own market.
I rise to a point of order. Surely it is absolutely unfair to refuse one hon. member permission to speak on a certain matter and then allow another hon. member to go on and deal with it.

He was
supposed to have been through.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the point of order raised by the hon. member for Huron-Perth (Mr. Golding) is well taken. I was about to rise and point out to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) that he was out of order, for the same reason that I considered the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) out of order.

I shall have to bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but I have been interested this afternoon to note that the only statements we have had from hon. members on the government side have been points of order, to try to shut off the discussion of one of the most important matters in western Canada to-day. If the minister will assure us that under item 12, possibly, we shall have an opportunity to discuss the question of the importation of vegetable oils, I shall be quite willing to leave it at that.

Looking
over the report of the department for last year I see that the work of the agricultural economics branch included a study of terminal market facilities for fruits and vegetables in the city of Toronto and a utilization of farm lands in Saskatchewan. Following what has been said by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the advisability of giving some study to the utilization of farm lands in Ontario. I quite realize that vast areas in the western provinces might be more effectively utilized, but I also believe that the utilization of great areas in the northern part of Ontario might be brought about by careful investigation and methodical research.

Supply-Agriculture-Economics

And southern Ontario
also.

Most of southern Ontario is being pretty well utilized now; however, I would appreciate an extension of the study into the southern parts as well. My hon. friend from Essex East (Mr. Martin) shakes his head, but it appears to me that a study of this kind in his own district would be of great importance. I am glad he utilizes much of his time in the interests of agriculture. No studies have been made so far as I know-at least we have not observed results from any-as to what different districts might accomplish in the way of greater economic production. I believe we have fallen far short throughout the whole dominion in the utilization of our vast agricultural areas. We are many years behind in having what might be termed a zoning policy, giving special study, consideration and encouragement to different districts to produce the crops to which they are most suited. I am glad to note that even in some parts of Peace River they believe they can produce vegetables, and with good reason, because I have seen some of their vegetables which are comparable to those produced in southern Ontario. Certain districts are more suited to the raising of live stock and to dairy production, while others are undoubtedly better suited to grain production. I see some hon. members smiling with pride when they think of the Ottawa valley and districts in eastern Ontario that are more adapted to live stock and dairy production, but there are districts in central Ontario which undoubtedly are more suited to the production of grain. Other districts in the western and northwestern part of lower Ontario are also adapted to the production of live stock, while in the south and southwestern part of the province there is land the rich soil of which might be utilized to greater advantage than it is at present.
I rose particularly, however, to bring to the attention of the minister the need for study of the utilization of agricultural lands in northern Ontario. In many parts of northern Ontario there are rich and fertile agricultural soils, but the climate is cold and the seasons short. I do believe that the constant, application of more scientific methods of production in many parts of northern Ontario which today are not giving returns sufficient to encourage agricultural development, would return a substantial improvement. This is all the more important in view of the steady development of the great mining industry.
It has been my privilege to visit northern Ontario, to see some of their excellent crops and to talk to men who have shown their

vegetables at the Canadian National Exhibition and the Royal Winter Fair. I talked to a man who in one year won a championship for potatoes produced in the community outside Timmins, where the season is short indeed. I have seen the excellent herds of dairy and beef cattle in northern Ontario, and have at the same time been reminded that consumers in that district are paying more for their meat and dairy products than are the consumers in southern Ontario, despite the fact that the farmers in the district who are struggling to establish herds and to promote agriculture are at times selling their beef cattle at prices lower than those received by farmers adjacent to Toronto. Cattle are shipped to Toronto, slaughtered and then shipped back to the mining districts of Timmins, Kirkland Lake and Sudbury, and the farmers who produce meat products in that part of the country are receiving much less than the farmers in southern Ontario. These are matters closely related to agricultural economics which might be considered by the economics branch of the Department of Agriculture.
The hon. member for Peace River has truly stated that the long freight hauls from British Columbia affect the consumption in his constituency of fruits and vegetables. A similar system of freight rates affects the dairy producers in western Canada. Some years ago western Canada produced only cereals of different kinds, and was not considered seriously in connection with the production of live stock and animal products, but we have lived to see the day when the value of dairy products in Canada has been substantially greater than the value of our wheat production. Although I am not sure of 1931 and 1933, I do know that in 1932 the value of dairy products was greater than that of wheat production. Some other hon. members may be more familiar than I am with dairy production in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba. But the economics branch in its report of last year recognized the importance of the establishment of terminal market facilities for fruits and vegetables in Toronto, and it must be of equal importance to study market conditions respecting other agricultural products which must be carried by long freight hauls.
When we know that it costs $1.86 per hundredweight to ship butter from the community surrounding Winnipeg to Toronto, that it costs $2.65 to ship from the Regina section of Saskatchewan and $3.33 from the Edmonton district of Alberta, we realize at once the importance of freight charges. The rates are correspondingly large to Montreal and other eastern centres. While I am not

Supply-Agriculture-Economics
deviating from the point at issue, or for the moment attempting to answer the hon. member for Huron North, I feel that if we who live in the southern and eastern parts of Canada are to reap the benefits of industrial development and advancement we must give careful study to that phase of agricultural economics which so directly affects the welfare and prosperity of the farmer in other districts. The figures indicate that one must pay $1.10 per hundredweight to ship lard from Winnipeg to Toronto, $1.45 to ship it from Regina and $1.76 from Edmonton. Tallows and other coarse fats are shipped at cheaper rates in tank cars. Vegetable oils are shipped in to Toronto and Montreal in tank carloads at twenty-five cents per hundredweight in competition with our animal products.
The minister may contend that I am deviating from the point at issue-
You have never reached it.
It may be by your tariff board.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to confine his observations to item 7. As points of order have been raised this afternoon I must ask that -he conform with the rules.

I shall be pleased to abide by your ruling; that is the reason I did not attempt to answer the hon. member for Huron North who, I suggest, deviated farther than I have from the point at issue. Agricultural economics with respect to marketing conditions are of vital importance. The hon. member for Peace River,
I submit, was quite in order when he mentioned freight rates in connection with the utilization of production within the dominion.
The economics branch of the department should long ere this have been directed to give more careful attention to the development of markets and the utilization of products in some sections of the country. This is a matter which, although not entirely divorced from the investigation by the tariff -board, is to some extent outside it. The other matters for the consideration of the board deal with specific items entering Canada, the wages paid, the processing, the standard of living and other matters relevant thereto. It is my firm belief that the economics branch should give careful consideration to the question whether some of the products which are regarded as not interfering or directly competing with live stock products or, in fact, are in actual competition with them.
51052-184J
We are capable of producing sufficient butter fat, lard, edible tallow and greases and oils to meet the requirements of the country. Eastern Canada alone could produce sufficient of these products to meet all requirements and, if it was profitable, western Canada could produce still more. We have 318,000 dairy farmers in Canada, all of ivhom are vitally concerned in this issue. If you ask these farmers in what branch of agricultural economics they are interested, they will reply that it is in the finding of better markets for their products. They are more interested in that than in any research as to what may be a better producing district than another.
Then the soya bean and linseed oil production should be considered. The hon. member for Essex East might give some study to the production of soya beans in his district.

I made a speech in the
house on that subject.

My hon.
friend made a speech on that matter. He also has a large automobile industry in his constituency which offers an enormous market for agricultural production.
The farmers could be helped still more by giving them cheaper automobiles.
If the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) can induce the chairman not to rule against me, I shall be glad to deal with that.

speechtext: Order.

I am
ordered by the Chair not to answer that question.
I should like like to see the production of soya beans and linseed oil increased, to the benefit of the agriculturists of this country. Some districts are more suitable for this type of production than others. We have the manufacturing equipment for the processing of these products. I urge upon the minister that a careful study be made of this matter, quite apart from the consideration being given to it by the tariff board. These issues vitally affect the agricultural prosperity of this dominion and concern the future welfare of the live stock industry of Canada. I say this in all seriousness and with no desire whatever to hold up the estimates.
I would not suggest that at all. This reminds me of one of the hon. member's speeches that lost Ontario.

The minister has mentioned election speeches, but all this is aside from the issue. If a careful study is not made of the effect of the importa-
Supply-Agriculture-Economics

tion and use of vegetable oils upon the production of animal products, a day will come when the old-line free traders who now shake their heads will regret that they did not stop such importations in time to save the government of the day from defeat.

Only thinking of the
old-time promises?

The farmers are the one class of people who have not an organization to present the facts of their case to a board of investigation. They have few organizations similar to those possessed by other producers or classes in the dominion. I believe that I speak to no small extent on behalf of hundreds of thousands of dairy farmers and other farmers when I say that in these times we cannot afford to lay our home markets open to the competition of tropical countries which can produce these things much more cheaply than we can. A careful study should be made of the effect of this competition and whether these products are entering markets which properly belong to the live stock industry, the basis of agriculture in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, no hon. member knows better than I do the justness and impartiality with which you preserve order in this committee. It is for that reason that I venture to rise to say a few more words upon a subject which I cannot permit to be dropped without further explanation. A moment ago I referred to the attempts being made to develop newer areas and to remove people from drought areas into other parts of the country. The great danger in doing this is that those who do not believe in such a plan are often prone to go about the country and say that those favouring the plan desire to drive the people from their homes, from the centres which they have known since childhood and from the places where their children have received their education. I do not believe that a scheme of this type should be carried out on a compulsory basis. I merely suggest that those who desire to avail themselves of this sort of hope for the future, if I may put it that way, should have at their command satisfactory knowledge as to what they will have to face. They should be supplied with the most accurate information as to what they may expect to find in the new areas.
This is a problem with which I am acquainted personally. Five years ago the United Farmers of Alberta government took people from the Sunnynook area and moved them up into the Peace River district. A large number of these people arrived one day
[Mr. W. E. Rowe.)
at Falher. where I reside, to establish themselves some twenty miles south of the town. They came from a district where they had been living year after year in the hope of having a crop. A decisive step had been taken on their behalf. I know that this must be most boring to many members of the committee.

I do not mind listening to speeches that have to do with the matter under discussion, but as I said before, this whole matter will come up under the vote for that purpose. If there is any more discussion on this item, we are prepared to listen to it, if not, I think we had better ask that the item stand.
Item stands.
Pensions and other benefits-civil pensions- Robert Allen, $269.52.

speakeroldname: Hon. IAN MACKENZIE (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, these and the following items on the same page are all for the payment of life pensions to civilian employees who sustained injuries in the discharge of their regular duties which resulted in permanent disability, also pensions to dependents of civilian employees who were killed in the discharge of their regular duties, the pensions being calculated on the basis of the provincial workmen's compensation acts in the various provinces. As these cases do not come under provincial or federal acts, these sums are voted every year.
May I ask in what connection these injuries were sustained?

On January 3, 1916, Mr. Allen, who ivas employed as a civilian truck driver for the mechanical transport branch, suffered an accident which resulted in a permanent disability. While he was driving a truck, the fly wheel burst into pieces, and the flying pieces struck him, breaking the bones of the ankle, also above the ankle in two places. As a result there is complete ankylosis of the ankle joint, with the foot at a right angle to the leg, and no active movement of the toes of the foot. The outer side of the foot is short almost two inches.

My question was asked because I have received letters claiming consideration by the government for wounds received during the strike of 1919 in Winnipeg. Is the minister able to inform the committee whether any such claims are being considered by the government?

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
In connection with the military personnel?
No; civilian.
It has not been drawn to my attention.
Is Mr. Allen still in the employ of the department?
No; he is not able to work, I understand.

Item agreed to.
Civil pensions-Florence Walker, $360.
Why are some amounts larger than others? Are these cases all incapacitated and unable to work?
The compensation is based on the scale provided by the compensation act in the province in which the injury took place.
It is on the same basis?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Militia services-Royal Military College, $381,500.
This item was discussed for a considerable time on Friday evening.

Item agreed to.
Cadet services, $139,500.
What are the amounts granted to each province?

The
amounts depend on the number trained in each province. I shall give the strength in the various provinces as of August 31, 1937; Nova Scotia, 1,526; Prince Edward Island, 885; New Brunswick, 1,561; Quebec, 49,866; Ontario, 21,531; Manitoba, 1,723; Saskatchewan, 851; Alberta, 1,151; British Columbia, 1,245; making a total of 80,339.
I see that pay and allowances are provided for all ranks. Is payment made to the cadets themselves or simply to the officers commanding?
There is a grant of one dollar made on behalf of each cadet between fifteen and eighteen years of age who qualifies.
Is there any allowance now for uniforms, as there used to be?
No.

Would the minister not consider restoring to an extent that assistance towards uniforms? I should be glad if he would. I personally come into the matter to the extent of being connected with a sea cadet corps in my own town, and there is another one close by. I appreciate the work done voluntarily by those connected with these corps, and the effect on the boys so trained. The expenses which have to be met come principally at the present time out of the pockets of the citizens, and it is quite right that this should be so in many instances, because they are related to the cadets, but I should like to see a little further assistance given by the department. Considering the trend of the times and the fact that the reductions were made when times were not as prosperous, shall I say, I wonder whether the minister would not seriously consider giving a little further assistance to the cadet services.

I shall be very glad indeed to take the suggestion of my hon. friend into careful consideration. The reductions were made in 1931, when conditions were extremely difficult. I quite agree with my hon. friend as to the valuable services performed in connection with the cadet movement, and that applies not only to the land cadets and the sea cadets but to the splendid services of the air cadets whom we have at Port Hope, and it is hoped that the air cadet service will be extended in the near future.
At what points in British Columbia are the cadet corps located at the present time?
There are twenty units in British Columbia as of August 31, 1937. I have not at the moment the locations of the stations.
How many units of sea cadets are there in Canada?
I shall get that for the next sitting. They are not separated in my book from the ordinary cadets.
What provisions are made for enabling the sea cadets to enter the Canadian navy?

They are given every possible preference. Some of them go on to the naval reserve after training, and their training stands them in good stead. They are given every encouragement and every possible preference.

How many sea cadets have gone into the Canadian navy?

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
I could not say at the moment.
At what age are they taken on?
At fifteen for cadets.	*
But at what age do they go into the navy? I think it is twenty.
They can join the regular Canadian navy as boy seamen at the age of seventeen. The grants for cadets are limited to those from fifteen to eighteen years of age.

Has the minister any intention of increasing this vote? Last year a number of us suggested that the vote be increased. I think it is one of the best votes we pass in this house. The cadet services have been most beneficial to this country, and from what the minister said last year I was hoping the vote would be increased this year.

I agree
with my hon. friend. The vote, of course, depends on the number of cadets who qualify for the grant. I regret to say that there has been a decrease in the last year in the number of cadets. Perhaps if the recognition suggested by the hon. member for Yale were again accorded it might improve the situation quite extensively.

Item agreed to.
Non-permanent active militia, $2,830,488.
There is a considerable increase in this vote. Will the increase be allotted among the units of the non-permanent forces to give them more training in camp?

Yes. Of the increase of $318,000, $250,000 is for additional training for all the units of the nonpermanent active militia. The actual time of training varies, according to the branch of the service, from about eleven days up to twenty-one days for some of the technical units for coastal defence.
Are they being trained with the most modern equipment?

Well, as far as the most modern equipment is available, they are. But at least they are trained in the theery of the most modern equipment. Some of that equipment is, of course, not yet available, but we are hoping to have it very soon.

I was talking a few days ago to one of the officers of a regiment here,

and I learned that that regiment is to go into camp for six days. I was led to believe that they would leave home on a Sunday and arrive home the following Sunday night, which is eight days, but they are to receive only six days' pay. The minister might well see that that does not happen. The non-permanent units are certainly giving great service to the country and are by no means adequately paid for the services they render. I do not think it is fair that the government should expect them to give two days of their time for nothing. I suggest that the minister should see to it that they get eight days' pay, or that they be paid from the time they leave home until the time they get back.

I am very glad to hear the observation of my hon. friend. I believe that the actual details in these matters are left very largely to the district officers commanding in the various military districts, but if there is any hardship in regard to any particular unit I should be very glad if hon. members will bring it to my attention. The general idea is to insist on at least five days' camp training. In previous years, largely owing to lack of funds, it was impossible to have much camp training; it was largely regimental and local training, but this year an endeavour is being made to insist upon camp training for all units.
This is not a complaint from the non-permanent forces.

Oh, I
understand that.
But I was given to understand that those are the facts in this particular case.
Will the minister explain this item of temporary assistance, $290,376?

I quite agree with the hon. member who has just spoken, about the attitude the non-permanent militia has taken during the last number of years as far as service to the country is concerned. I know personally from seeing many officers and men that they have devoted their time during the years of depression with very little remuneration. I should like to ask the minister with reference to reserve battalions in the different units. As he probably knows, there are many officers put on reserve units when they are still quite young and could be of great value to the service. There is no use made of them in our non-permanent force. The active battalions go into camp and get their training. Yet some of the best trained officers we have, whose training has entailed a lot of expense as far as the country is concerned as well as a good deal of expense to themselves personally, are not utilized in any way. It occurred to me that it might be possible for the minister to devise some way in which they could be employed with benefit to the militia and to the country. Has the minister anything in mind with regard to that matter?

As a matter of fact that very point was brought to my attention a while ago by some of the militia officers. A memorandum was directed to the department with respect to the question. Certainly it is to be regretted that these men, at a comparatively early age, cannot be utilized except by giving the benefit of their advice and experience to the active units. The question of utilizing their services certainly deserves consideration. Of course if an emergency should arise these highly trained men are available.
What steps are being taken to create anti-aircraft units?

Steps have been taken with regard to the establishment and the training of anti-aircraft units in the dominion. Unfortunately we are handicapped by the fact that orders placed by my predecessor in 1935 for anti-aircraft guns have not yet been filled. For reasons which I have no doubt my hon. friend realizes it has not been found possible to supply them. In regard to the theory of training, we have anti-aircraft units, their establishment is complete, and they are receiving training.

I am afraid that these units which are trained in theory only will not be much use in defending the country when it comes to destroying bombers and so on. Would the minister say just what equipment it is that we have not got with which to train our defence forces?

I think it is reasonably accurate to say that the training carried out in Canada compares very favourably at the present time with the training carried out in the territorial forces in England. I have authentic reasons for making that statement. Of course we have not got so far the most modern types of equipment, and in some cases that does constitute a handicap in regard to training. The two most pronounced types of equipment which are lacking to-day are, first, anti-aircraft guns, and second, the most modern type of heavy ordnance with the most modem mountings. Those are the two principal deficiencies in equipment.
What about machine guns, also searchlights and equipment of that kind?

We have some supplies of various types of machine guns for training purposes. Of course the Lewis gun is now practically obsolescent or obsolete. We have a supply of Vickers guns and several more on order, and as my hon. friend knows, as regards the new type of gun we are taking steps now to supply our forces with it.

Are there not also tank
battalions ?
Yes. If my memory serves me correctly there are six.
Have we tanks in Canada?
We have armoured cars, which take the place of tanka for demonstration and drill purposes.
Can we not procure tanks for training purposes?

They
have been ordered some time ago.

In regard to these different articles of equipment that are on order is there any reason why they cannot be manufactured in Canada, or why steps should not be taken at once to get ourselves in a position to manufacture them in Canada?

That has been very carefully considered.
Supply-Defence-M ilitia
It does not seem to get very far. Are our manufacturing plants unable to manufacture goods of this kind?
I should think they would be able.
When is it expected that we shall be able to obtain at least enough to train our troops with?
I think that before very long we shall have tanks available in Canada.
I take it item 184 or 185 would be the item under which to inquire further into the question of contracts for tanks and equipment generally?
Yes.

I noticed recently that the minister attended a dinner in Montreal and spoke to employers of labour, soliciting their assistance in facilitating employees going to camps. To what extent has that been successful? Have any further developments taken place, and were employers of labour ready to grant such facilities on full time?

On February 7 last I addressed a circular letter to the boards of trade and chambers of commerce throughout Canada, which I might read. It is as follows:
I should like to bring to attention a very important matter concerning preparation for the defence of Canada in time of war or emergency real or apprehended, and am taking the liberty of addressing this circular letter to boards of trade, chambers of commerce and other organizations through which can be reached those who employ members of the non-permanent active militia, the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve and the nonpermanent squadrons of the Royal Air Force.
Officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the Royal Navy, the permanent active militia and the Royal Canadian Air Force are competent and efficient but, as you well know, relatively very few in number. Man power which would be required in time of emergency or war would be drawn from the non-permanent forces.
The immediate purpose of this letter concerns the training of the non-permanent forces. Given that young Canadians in sufficient numbers offer to serve with the non-permanent forces, which indeed is the case, it becomes necessary to train them and this is carried out by members of the permanent forces.
Training of personnel of the non-permanent active militia, for instance, is carried out at local headquarters of the regiments or units. In the summer, training is carried out at military camps at different points throughout the country. Employers of non-permanent active militia personnel will grant that the training at local headquarters, usually carried out in

the evening, does not disturb the ordinary course of work or employment. It may be somewhat different when the employee asks leave or absence in order to attend militia training camp.
The non-permanent active militia is the first line of Canada's land defences. It is to these officers, non-commissioned officers and men that Canada must look for national security. It is submitted that these soldiers are deserving of all possible assistance and encouragement. Speaking on their behalf, I would earnestly request the sympathetic consideration of employers in making it possible for members of the non-permanent active militia to train without feeling that their positions or employment may be adversely affected by such patriotic action.
It would be greatly appreciated if the gentlemen to whom this letter is addressed would extend their cooperation by bringing this request to the notice of all members.
That letter has had a very encouraging response from all over Canada. Active committees are at work amongst employers, and already instructions have been given byseveral large firms to encourage their employees to attend summer training camps, with the assurance that there is no danger of their wages being interfered with. In other words a feeling of security has been given, and I think that will be of great assistance to the non-permanent forces.
To what extent has the reorganization of the non-permanent active militia been carried out?

I think in regard to personnel of units it is practically completed. There may be some units of the technical services not entirely completed. The difficulty of course is to get the necessary equipment for training purposes.
What is the authorized peace establishment of the non-permanent militia, and what is the actual strength at the present time?
The peace establishment as of June, 1937, was 85,982 and the strength was 45,631, but I happen to know that the training strength for the current year is 46,840.
The peace establishment is shown in the last report of the department as 7,647 officers and 91,938 other ranks. Has that been reduced in the last year?

As my hon. friend knows, the paper strength was reduced at the time of the reorganization. I think we had a paper strength before the reorganization of 120,000, and that was reduced to about 90,000 at the time of reorganization
