because certain units went out of existence and smaller units of a technical nature were formed in their place.

The last report of the department is dated March 31, 1937; at that time the authorized peace establishment was over 99,000. The minister says that at the present time the peace establishment is 85,000. Has there been a reduction of 15,000 in the last year?

The
figures I gave were as of June 30, 1937. Of course these would not be the figures at the present time.

How does the minister
account for the discrepancy between the figures on page 98 of the last annual report and the figures he gives as of June, 1937?

The
correct figures would not be those shown at the end of the fiscal year. These figures are entirely paper strength, and not material in regard to the actual strength of the units.
What is the actual strength of the permanent and non-permanent militia on the Pacific coast?

For
military district No. 11 as of June 30, 1937, the non-permanent numbered 3,249. The permanent force on March 31 of the present year was 31 officers and 299 other ranks; total, 330.
What proportion of the nonpermanent militia is in the interior of the province-that is, would not be available for coastal defence?
I would not admit that they would not all be available for coastal defence. We consider that those in the interior would be available practically at once in any emergency.

It seems obvious that in order to defend the coast we must have enough soldiers to man the fortifications and protect naval and air bases and also if necessary to repel raids. Does the minister think the forces he has on the Pacific coast at the present time are ample for that purpose?
Of course if there were an emergency on either coast the theory of the staff is that all the militia in Canada would be available very quickly.

This as the minister knows is a very serious question for the people residing on the Pacific slope. Does the minister
think that the militia strength in British Columbia at the present time is sufficient to protect the people of the province? Apparently it is not recruited even up to peace strength. Would it not be possibls to recruit the units further until we have enough men there to do the job?
Recruiting has increased to a very encouraging extent in British Columbia.

But is an attempt being
made to bring the units there up even to peace strength, and if not does the minister not think it should be done?

Every
possible encouragement is being given to recruiting; a special effort is being made not only in British Columbia but all over Canada, and I think the results are encouraging.
Could the department supply equipment and officers for the full peace establishment of the British Columbia units under the vote which is going through at the present time?
My hon. friend is speaking of the non-permanent active militia?
Yes, the non-permanent.

I can
assure my hon. friend that nothing has been done by the department to retard recruiting.

I am asking if anything has been done by the department to bring the strength of the British Columbia units up to the peace time establishment. I understand they are thousands below it at the present time

Of course, if there was any need for it we could have ample forces moved to British Columbia in very short order. It is not anticipated by anyone that the forces actually on either coast at present would be ample in case there should be a real emergency. That is not a theory upon which any system of defence is built up, because obviously it would be unworkable.

Are there enough soldiers
in the province even to man the fortifications that are being built, and to protect the bases?
Enough are available and their positions in that regard are very carefully assigned.
Item agreed to.

Supply-Defence-Permanent Force
Permanent force, $6,087,760.

I notice a moderate
increase in this permanent force vote. Bearing in mind that the principal use of the permanent force in peace time is to train the skeleton force which we know as the nonpermanent active militia, and that this force recently has been reorganized and must be trained in the use of more modem weapons and equipments, remembering also that money is being spent on defence works on the Pacific coast, does the minister really think there is a sufficient increase in the permanent force vote to take care of that work?

I agree with my hon. friend immediately that at present the members of the permanent force are exceedingly hard worked in regard to the duties they have to perform by way of giving the necessary instruction to the non-permanent active militia. Of course it is very difficult for me to answer the question categorically. Personally I should have liked to see a further increase in the vote for the permanent force, for the purpose of carrying out these instructional duties; but after a careful balancing of the available resources, this small increase was finally agreed upon.

The minister is no doubt aware of the fact that with the completion of the batteries being erected on the Pacific coast it will be necessary for sections of the permanent force to reside in those neighbourhoods, because I assume he will not leave the guarding of those emplacements to the nonpermanent active miltia; it will have to be done by permanent force men. That will take away a certain number of officers and men from their other duties of training the non-permanent active militia, and I greatly question whether, remembering the work that falls on the permanent force at the present time, the minister has sufficient at his disposal for that purpose.

My hon. friend is quite correct in regard to the duties of guarding these emplacements, which in ordinary times will take some of the personnel of the permanent force away from their other duties, but the non-permanent force is assigned the duty of actually manning these emplacements if any emergency should arise.

Quite so, and we all hope the emergency will not arise; but the guns and emplacements cannot be just left without any guard at all, and I should imagine that guard will have to come from the permanent force.
Yes; I think that will be the arrangement.

I have been informed that the delay in the delivery of airplanes to the Canadian government-and incidentally to the transport service-is being occasioned by a large order for planes for the government of Japan. To-day the Toronto Star carries a story from its Ottawa correspondent, Mr. Lipsett, to the effect that an order for thirty planes has been placed in Canada by the Japanese government, and that this is likely to interfere seriously with the delivery of planes both to the government and to the trans-Canada air service. Can the minister tell us anything about this?

I was not aware of the news dispatch to which my hon. friend refers; but I can tell him immediately that those firms building airplanes for the government of Canada have not had any orders retarded, as far as my knowledge goes, as a result of any orders for airplanes for Japan. As a matter of fact, at the present moment I can make the statement that I do not think any of the firms building planes for this government have such an order; if they have, it has not come to my notice. I could give from memory the names of the firms that are building planes for this government, and as far as any information at my disposal goes they have not received an order from Japan.
Would the minister give the names of those firms?

There is Canadian Vickers, in Montreal; Fairchild, in Montreal; the Noorduyn company, Montreal; the Ottawa Car Company, Ottawa; the de Havilland company, Toronto; the National Steel Car Corporation of Canada, Hamilton; the Fleet company, for training purposes, in Fort Erie, and the Boeing company, now converted to a Canadian company in Vancouver.

We have a British mission in Canada at the present time, I believe, looking over the ground for the purchase of airplanes in Canada, and it strikes me that this is another matter which might be considered by the department owing to the international situation. Also in to-day's newspapers there is the story of the bombing of a Canadian Baptist mission by Japanese planes, and it seems to me we shall be placed in rather ah unfortunate position if Canadian firms are to supply Japan with planes that may be used

for such purposes, particularly if they are likely to interfere with the delivery of the planes for which money has been appropriated by this parliament or the parliament of the mother country. I bring that to the attention of the minister and the government.

Thank
you.
What firms are making planes now for shipment to Japan?
I have no information at all.

If I might I should like to ask one further question with regard to the non-permanent active militia. Last winter I heard complaints to the effect that the militiamen were not supplied with boots, and that in many instances this kept men from enlisting, because they did not feel that they should buy heavy boots which would be of no use to them in civil life. Is it a fact that the militia men are not supplied with boots by the government?

As far as my information goes, the members of the nonpermanent active militia never have been supplied with boots by any government in Canada. I quite agree with my hon. friend that there is at the present time a strong feeling among the militia that they should be supplied with boots for summer camp purposes and also for ordinary training purposes, and although no definite decision has been arrived at, the matter has been receiving some attention in the department within the last month or two.
Are there any factories making airplanes in Canada besides those mentioned by the minister?

Oh, I
think so; but not for us. There is one factory in Fort William, I understand, manufacturing airplanes, but not for the Canadian government.
Are they not in a position to manufacture quite a large number of airplanes in the Fort William area?
Speaking quite unofficially, I understand so.
Is it not possible that they may be making airplanes for the Japanese?

I am
speaking entirely without knowledge, of course; that is possible, but I do not know.

Before
those airplanes could be shipped out, there would have to be a permit issued by the department, would there not?

That
would be a matter for the Department of National Revenue, in regard to the section of the Customs Act dealing with war materials; I think it is section 290.
Supposing those were commercial airplanes which could be converted into military planes; would they come under the government ban concerning the shipment of goods for war purposes?
That would be entirely a matter of policy for the Minister of National Revenue.
Is it not a policy of the government also?
Not in 'egard to the export of planes.

Is a licence required
for the export of these planes? We are not recognizing any war between China and Japan.
I think a licence is required. Of course this does not come under my department, and in these answers I am speaking subject to correction.
Perhaps the Prime Minister would tell us?

They have to have a licence?

Engineer services and works, $2,483,500.

Probably this is the item under which the minister would like to discuss the issuance of contracts. This involves a consideration of weapons and equipment of all sorts. My feeling, and one which I believe is widely felt, is that at least four years ago Canada was officially aware of the fact that the supplying of materials and equipment in Great Britain would prevent firms over there from being able to deliver orders from Canada and other dominions within a reasonable space of time. Shortly after this government took office we were informed that the minister was making an intensive survey of industrial concerns in Canada to find out what factories there were, and what extensions might be made for this purpose. Now that we are in the year 1938 the public is beginning to wonder how
Supply-Defence-Engineers

much information has been collected on the subject, and to what extent it is possible to employ Canadian workmen in Canadian factories for the supplying of this very much needed equipment. Would the minister give in some detail a description of the investigations he has made, and state to what extent contracts are already in their hands?

The
investigation to which the hon. member refers comes under the next item respecting general stores. Some eighteen months ago an industrial survey was commenced under the direction of the master general of the ordnance. Speaking in round figures, I believe about 700 firms in various parts of Canada have been surveyed with reference to their potential capacity for production in any particular direction in the event of a national emergency. The procedure followed was that expert engineers-sometimes one and sometimes two of them-visited the plants and brought back thorough and comprehensive reports with recommendations as to what the potential capacity of an industry might be. At the present time these reports are being codified and correlated in the department, so that we shall have available a complete list of all the firms in Canada. The last figure I have shows that there are 768 firms. I believe I said in the first instance that there were 700. The greater figure brings the list up to date, and includes the whole of Canada.
In addition to this, a complete list has been prepared in the department showing the various implements and types of equipment which can now be manufactured or produced in Canada. Second, we have a list of the various types of equipment which could be produced in Canada as a result of further development, such as government cooperation with industry, or the government operating on its own initiative. Third, we have a list of those types of equipment which cannot be produced in Canada. I refer to such equipment as heavy armour-piercing shells, the manufacturing of which requires the highest form of technical skill and many years of experience.
Were they not made in Canada during the war?

I believe towards the end of the war there was a commencement made in that direction; at least that is my recollection, but I am not sure. In any case those classifications have been made.
In regard to the actual procurement may I say that since the house last met, in regard to munitions there was an order given to a

civilian firm in Montreal which is now manufacturing shells. If I remember correctly, the order was for 30,000 shells. As I stated some time ago, the main handicap is in connection with the heavy calibre guns and the modern high angle mountings which, of course, greatly increase the range of guns.
Briefly speaking, that has been the result up to date. I wish to state frankly, however, that possibly it will be necessary to go further in connection with the question of procurement. It W'ould appear to become more obvious all the time that it will be necessary in Canada to rely upon our own production and manufacturing resources for the procurement of equipment essential to meet a national emergency.
The minister referred to the 768 firms which might be used in the event of a national emergency. My point is this: Why are we not now proceeding-
I should have used the words, " prepare for a national emergency."

Why are we not now proceeding to produce some of these things? For instance, it is perfectly well known that all Canada has been able to get in the way of Bren guns has been a very small number for purposes of demonstration. Why have we not a contract at this time in some factory-[DOT]
We have.
The minister says that we have. Would he give information with respect to it?

May I refer to some notes I have with reference to the matter? As far back as the summer of 1936 the Department of National Defence came to the conclusion that it would be necessary to arm the forces with the Bren gun, and that 7,000 of these guns would be required. A few model or specimen Bren guns were ordered, and it early became clear that Canada could not look to the manufacturing establishments of the government of the United Kingdom as a certain or timely source of supply reasonably safe from possible enemy action. The two model guns which we now have were made not in England but in Czechoslovakia where they were invented; the Enfield plant near London cannot satisfy the United Kingdom government's requirements before several years. The fact that the United Kingdom is not only willing but anxious to order 5,000 Bren guns from a Canadian manufacturer is of utmost significance. We received direct advice to this effect from the War Office.

Supply-Defence-Engineers
This memorandum was prepared before the actual contract was let. In view of the situation then existing it was deemed advisable to consider the possible necessity of having our requirements manufactured in Canada. The probable difficulties of the position of the United Kingdom were surmised here from the beginning. Because of known variations in cost factors, heavy outlays for machinery that would be required if the guns were to be manufactured in Canada, it was known that Canadian production costs would be more than English production costs; if only 7,000 guns were to be made in Canada, it was believed that the cost would be prohibitive under normal conditions. Such has turned out to be the case, to the extent that the placing of the 5,000 order in Canada will save something more than 11,000,000 in cash to Canadian taxpayers. It is impossible to translate into dollars the other advantages to Canada in regard to extending our means of defence.
Therefore the Canadian government has let a contract for 7.000 Bren guns to a firm in Toronto, the John Ingiis Company Limited. I believe it is. Then, the War Office directly and not through the Canadian government has given a contract to the same firm for 5,000 guns. The terms of the contract were very carefully analysed and examined for over three months by the interdepartmental committee on profits, and a subcommittee of the main one gave special attention to the matter. Various suggestions were made and possibilities examined with respect to government plants, and in connection with various other methods of carrying out the contract. The contract, which I shall be pleased to place before the committee, was entered into on, roughly speaking, a basis of ten per cent cost plus. The War Office contract is on exactly the same terms and conditions as the one with the Canadian government. From information available in the department it appears that the War Office have expressed themselves as being satisfied with the terms of the contract entered into with this Canadian company in Toronto. In Australia they have a Bren plant which is publicly owned. That plant has been constructed I believe, for two or two and a half years, but they have not yet got into production. I am subject to correction when I say that in England the Enfield company were two and a half years before they got into production, but they are now producing fifty Bren guns a week. A guarantee has been given that the Canadian company will be in production within twenty-four months. As a result of the separate orders from England and from ourselves, the actual saving will be $1,3SO,000.
We are using much of the plant which we had in storage in Canada, and there will be a considerable saving on capital cost of machinery, probably to the extent of $250,000.

That is the machinery
which was in storage at Valcartier?
Yes.

It is being used by this
Ingiis company?
Machinery is being supplied by each of the two governments, the Canadian government paying for two-thirds of the cost and the War Office paying one-third. The ownership remains with this government.

Have any
contracts been given out by the government on a cost plus basis?

If my
memory is correct, there are six.
What are the different firms?

The particulars of the contracts are as follows:
1.	18 Bristol "Bolinbroke" aircraft, contract given to the Fairchild Aircraft Company, Montreal.
2.	11 Blackburn "Shark" aircraft, contract to the Boeing Aircraft Company, Vancouver.
3.	12 Lysander aircraft, to the National Steel Car Company, Hamilton.
4.	Battery at Albert Head, British Columbia. Contract given to the Northern Construction Company and E. J. Ryan, Vancouver.
5.	30,000 shells, 20,000 of one calibre and 10,000 of another, to the Montreal Construction Supply and Equipment Company, Limited, Montreal.
6.	Bren gun contract, 7,000 and 5,000 to the John Ingiis Company, Toronto.
Reconditioning 18 Wapiti aircraft, Ottawa Car Company, Ottawa.
35 trucks, four-wheeled, 15 hundredweight, with spare tires, tubes and canvas covers, General Motors Limited, Oshawa.
Were there any other firms that could have done the work covered by these contracts?

These
contracts represent a very small part of the total amount of the contracts let. In other instances contracts were let by tender, either through public advertising or from selected lists. In all these instances the contracts were carefully scrutinized by the interdepartmental committee, and with one exception it was known that in each instance a competitive tender was impossible. The contract for the Albert Head work was let in this way because of military secrecy.

According to the particulars on page 133 of the estimates there is a decrease of about SI ,300,000 in the vote for buildings and works. I suppose the works referred to have to do mainly with gun emplacements and fortifications on the western coast. I believe the minister told us some time ago that these works were in the second stage of development.
Yes.

I should like to know what amounts are being apportioned for the preparation of defence works on the eastern coast. We hear so much about the defence of the west coast that I am afraid the minister might forget that we have an eastern coast to Canada, and that the western coast is not the only part which requires defence.

Most of the work being done on the Atlantic coast under the estimates this year is in connection with the air force vote. I shall be glad to give my hon. friend the details of the money expended under that vote when it is reached. For certain obvious reasons special consideration has .been given to the Pacific coast, but I assure my hon. friend that this is not because the minister comes from there. This work is being done because of a definite recommendation by the general staff and others who are advising the department with reference to these matters. I can assure my hon. friend that there is no intention of neglecting the defence of the eastern coast.
Is it the intention of the department to start these defences this year?
Only with reference to air defences.
At what points?
Dartmouth, Yarmouth, Truro and Sydney.

Those points are all in Nova Scotia, to which fact I have no objection. However, Saint John is one of the great ports of Canada. It is one of the focal points, so far as trade is concerned, and it seems to me there should be some development in connection with the defence of New Brunswick. Some time ago I suggested that use should be made of Sussex, the local training area in New Brunswick. I hope the minister will consider some development along these lines in New Brunswick.

I shall be glad to remember what my hon. friend has said. A very definite plan has been prepared in connection with Saint John defences.

My recollection is that the recommendation was made that the air defences to be provided at Nova Scotia points would prove an effective defence for Saint John as well. That does not apply to the local defence of Saint John, in connection with which careful plans have been drawn up.
Will any of this item be devoted for that purpose?
This is for air defences only.
Are we to have anything in the way of gun emplacements at Saint John, or anything else of that nature?
I do not think so as yet.
The minister must have the information.
I do not think there is.
What is the present position with regard to the fortifications at Albert Head, the York island battery and other fortifications on the Pacific coast?

The

There are three units making up the personnel of the Canadian navy. First, there is the permanent force which includes those men who make the navy their profession; second, the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve which is composed of men who make their living from the sea, such as fishermen and men in the merchant marine; third, the Royal Canadian Voluntary Naval Reserve which is composed of men who have a liking for the sea.
I understand the permanent naval force is to be increased this year, and I think it would be well if the young people of our country knew the conditions of enlistment in the Canadian navy. However, what I am particularly interested in at the present time is the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve. I understand that this force has an authorized strength of 500 men and officers but that there are only 240 in it at the present time. The age limits for enlistment are eighteen to thirty years. A man who joins this force as a naval reservist is given S45 a year as a retaining fee, as it were. He trains six weeks during his first year of service, for which he receives on the average $1.80 a day. This works out to about $100 a year. The opportunity to earn an extra $100 a year may be very attractive to a young fisherman on the

coast of Nova Scotia. The course of training would also improve his seamanship and benefit him mentally and physically and at the same time he would be cooperating in a scheme for the defence of the Canadian coast.
I submit that schools for the training of men who enroll in the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve should be established in the seaport towns of Nova Scotia. The training is done during the off season. There are armouries in many of the towns along the sea coast, especially in the riding which I represent. I realize the mechanics of the problem would have to be worked out by the technical naval officers of the department, but I believe if naval instructors and equipment were supplied these schools could be carried on with very little expense.
It occurs to me that there should be coordination between the Department of Labour, with its troubles in connection with employment, and the naval and militia branches. Earlier in the discussion of these estimates we were told that in the air service it takes seven men on the ground to maintain one man in the air. I consider it most important that we should manufacture as much as possible of the material used for defence purposes. When we manufacture airplanes we are creating technically trained labour which would be available should the need for defence ever arise. In the meantime we are providing employment in civil life. We are creating future artisans to take their place in the civil life of the country.
Years ago the defence of the country was a different matter. The farmer, for instance, who lived on a farm was usually a good horseman, and his horse provided the best method of transport. He had his rifle and was a good shot, also a good scout, and so the farmers made a splendid unit of defence. But that has changed. The defence of the country is subject to the changes progress has brought in other directions. Science demands that you must train men in the laboratories for defence; also in our industrial plants, where machinists and mechanical engineers are at work, we find a training field for the youth of Canada that is especially valuable and very desirable. It seems to me that if the Department of National Defence would cooperate with the Department of Labour in every way possible they would be able to train men for the engineering trades in our industrial plants, and this would also help the unemployment situation. Industry in this country should assume some part of the burden, and it might well be required to train men in the indus-[Mr. Kinley.l
trial plants of Canada. I once suggested to the Minister of Labour that we might even go so far as to have subsidized apprenticeships so that our young men might be trained for some skilled work which they could follow as they grow older, because it is well known that when a young man gets up to be twenty-one or twenty-two without any objective he is inclined to become a drifter instead of helping out in industry.
I think men could be trained, particularly for the naval service. Our fishermen are good pilots, skilled in the handling of boats, and resourceful. This training will improve their condition; it would mean for young men more earning power and give them a better standing in their profession. I trust the minister will explore the situation fully. I know he has already looked into the possibilities, and I hope he will explore them further with particular reference to the Atlantic coast.
The Royal Naval Reserve is to a large extent built up from the merchant marine. They have a flag. It will be recalled that we had a discussion in this house this session about a national flag for Canada. The merchant marine may fly the naval reserve flag, which is the blue ensign, with the coat of arms of Canada on the fly. In order that this flag may be flown, a certain number of the crew must be naval reserve men, and the ships that are permitted to fly it consider it an honour. The old idea was that if the ship had a gun crew they could fly this flag. The flag is flown by some of the boats of the Canadian merchant marine. The flag, to seamen, has a language all its own, and is very important.
We have heard a great deal about how vulnerable the Atlantic coast is to attack. Our distance from European powers, however, is an element for safety because enemy craft upon the sea or under the sea and in the air are handicapped in working a long way from their base. In the autumn of 1937 it came to the department's attention that the contractor was seriously involved financially. Would the minister give some idea as to the purpose of our air force in Canada?

While I shall not answer at length, it has been said in general debate that an air force is not primarily for defensive purposes. I must say that the advice I have received from those supposed to be qualified to advise is to the opposite effect. They say an air force can be as effective in defence as it may be in offence. So far as the plans drawn up in the Department of National Defence are concerned, may I say that the entire purpose of the air force is to combine, according to carefully prepared plans, with the land force, if necessary, and with our small sea force for the protection of our focal areas, our trade routes and our coastal areas and, if we were neutral, for the protection of our neutrality.

The minister has mentioned the protection of our neutrality. A matter occurs to me which, I believe, has not yet been discussed in the house. Within the last few days we have heard a great deal as to the possibility of Canada supplying planes or other munitions of war to Great Britain. In that case I fancy it might very well be that the first objective of any attacking force would be the factories in which such aeroplanes or war materials are being produced. In such event I fancy it would be difficult to protect our neutrality. It would be difficult to remain neutral if we were actively engaged in supplying materials of war to any nation, whether it be a British nation or a nation outside the empire. I should like to ask whether or not any arrangement has been arrived at by which no materials would be manufactured in or exported from Canada without a licence from the Department of National Defence, and whether in the granting of such licence consideration will be given to the added dangers which, it seems to me, would come to Canada because of the manufacture in this country of munitions of war.

Do I understand that the requirements for topographic surveys are still furnished by the Department of National Defence?

Yes; we do the photographic work. I have a detailed description of the operations. The requirements of air survey take the Royal Canadian Air Force from coast to coast and from the United States boundary to the arctic circle, and the demand for new work is always greater than can possibly be accomplished. In 1937 the Royal Canadian Air Force detachment photographed from the air a total of 77,500 square miles. The photographic season is from the time the snow melts to the first snowfall of the following winter. Last year because the snow did not arrive until December the aircraft were kept on photography a month later than usual, with the result that the work which normally is done in the winter, such as overhauling aircraft engines and cameras, had to be hastened in order to get the aircraft out to their work in the west where the snow disappears earlier than in the east. How many officials in the department were employed in gathering these quantities of vegetables?

There was no extra staff at this end; it was all done by the regular staff. It was under Mr. Wheeler, who was in charge of the branch, and our regular inspectors made the inspections and carried out the work.

Did they receive offers from wholesalers to ship the fruit, vegetables, fish, beans and so on, before they undertook to gather them in this way?
Supply-Agriculture-M arke ting

Quotations were obtained from different vegetable and fruit marketing organizations, but it was thought advisable to purchase as directly as we could from those who had surpluses of these commodities. For example, down in the Holland marsh area, where it was not possible for the people to dispose of the vegetables grown there, we purchased a considerable amount. The main reason for not dealing with wholesalers at both ends was the fact that we were purchasing commodities which, in the ordinary course of events, would not have found their way into these homes. The individuals in the relief areas were supplied with schedules providing for a certain amount per month, which was covered by vouchers to the merchants. These vouchers covered those things which were considered to be absolute necessities. We have had considerable difficulty in the past, particularly in farm homes throughout the drought areas, because the merchants did not carry certain of these things. They had no opportunity to sell them, and the vouchers were not sufficient to permit of that kind of thing being purchased. We had in mind the idea of providing certain commodities that otherwise would not be purchased. In addition, we thought this provided an opportunity of placing these commodities in homes where they were not ordinarily consumed. We selected the best of these commodities. The best British Columbia apples were selected, the best cheese and the best cured fish was obtained. Many of these homes had not been large users of these commodities for many years. It was considered that this was money well spent for advertising. These commodities were being placed before the people of this area, and it was thought that they would be larger purchasers later on as a result of this being done.

Why did the department
or the minister decide that in many places in Saskatchewan the distribution should be general? He just made the statement that these commodities were placed in homes where they were not generally used, but in many cases the distribution was general.

There was a general
distribution to those who considered that they needed these supplies. There was no check up to the extent that deliveries were made only to those on relief. The first reason for this was the belief that many people could be kept off relief by having these additional supplies. I believe many

did stay off relief as a result of having vegetables in their cellars and a little fish and cheese in their pantries. The other reason was advertising. These people were given these supplies as an advertisement. It was felt that they would not be shipped in at all if they were not shipped in in this way. The hon. member suggests that these supplies were delivered to everyone. There was a restriction placed against persons who were receiving regular salaries, such as bank managers and station agents. I dare say there were some exceptions, as is bound to happen in deliveries of this kind. However, those who felt themselves in need and who applied were given these supplies without too much check being made upon the situation existing in their homes.

I have not the correspondence with me at the moment as I did not expect we would reach this item, but I have letters from secretaries of municipalities enclosing copies of a letter that went out from Doctor Stapleford stating that there was to be a general distribution and that this suggestion came from the minister. I know of places where distribution was made to bankers, lawyers, butchers, hotel keepers and people of that sort. In some instances the people refused to accept the supplies. I should like to know how the minister arrived at the quantity required, even assuming that distribution was to be general. Just a minute ago the minister said that they had thirty-five carloads of beans. How did they arrive at that quantity? A grocer told me that was more beans than would be consumed in Saskatchewan in three years. I have also been told by a grocery firm that the prices paid for beans was in the neighbourhood of a dollar a sack more than the price for which they could have supplied them. Could the minister tell us what price was paid for beans, where they were gathered and how the quantity was arrived at? There are certain members who come from the districts in Ontario where beans are grown and they could compare the prices.

The beans were bought at SI.30 which was the lowest price that could be secured by anyone. The cost of shipping would be lower to the government than to a merchant because we were shipping in carload lots and at half rates. I do not think it would have been possible to supply the beans for a dollar less. The amounts supplied to a family of five were thirty pounds of cheese, thirty-three pounds of beans, one hundred and fifty pounds of apples, forty-four pounds of fish,

I had an experience similar to that of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. I found that in certain areas these foods were distributed without regard to whether people needed them. I made a protest, and the answer I received was that the federal regulations did not state whether or not a person had to be in need in order to receive the food.
The reason I protested was that in the marginal areas adjacent to the federal drought area there was a great deal of distress, and apparently the people in that area were not eligible for the distribution of these supplies. I protested, and the answer I received was that the people outside the federal drought area, no matter how much distress there might be, were not eligible for the distribution of this food.

There was some difficulty at the beginning, and complaints came in from the area immediately adjacent to what was known as the federal drought area where we were taking care of the people 100 per cent. An attempt was made to take care of that situation by inducing the voluntary committee to make their distributions in the area outside rather than inside the federal area. There was some difficulty experienced in having that done because there were instances where people had expressed the desire to have their carload go to a particular section, and of course where any desire was expressed to have a car that was being sent gratis to western Canada distributed in a certain place, that was done. There were other instances of church organizations having directed cars to certain places, and it was impossible to change their destination. But we tried so to distribute the voluntary relief that was given as to assist those round about the federal area to greater advantage than those who were being assisted inside that area. We depended entirely on the local authorities to make the distribution, and I would say that in 90 per cent of the cases at any rate the distribution was carried out in the very best possible manner. In other cases there may have been some misunderstanding on the part of the local authorities as to just what was to be done with the commodities, and there might have been some distribution made where probably, if we had restricted them by regulation, distribution would not have been made; but I do not think any great harm was done or any great loss sustained as a result, I think it will be found that most people, as was stated by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley), who did not feel they were entitled to the goods did not take them. That was the case over the greater part of the area.

Was any part of the fruR and vegetables that were supplied by charitable organizations distributed in the federal area?
Supply-Agriculture-Marketing

In Alberta the provincial authorities asked us not to make any distribution of vegetables because they had sufficient vegetables to take care of the situation in the federal area in that province, but there was a certain section that was taken into the federal area in Alberta by special arrangement with the province. We had selected forty-two municipalities that we thought should go into the federal area. They made representations to the effect that there should be fifty-three. We questioned that, and a compromise was arrived at, the amount of the cash grant to the Alberta government to take care of the area outside the federal area being cut in two. When it came to the distribution of the food we suggested, in the first instance, that we would confine the distribution to forty-two municipalities. They proposed that they would make a distribution of vegetables over the whole area provided we covered the complete area with the other commodities, and that was done.
Does the minister consider that all this great quantity of food was essential out there, and that it was well used, or was a large quantity not required and therefore wasted?

I think anyone who has been through that area would agree that there was very little food wasted in that area this year. There were more people going short of food than wasting any food in the drought area last winter.
Was any distribution of potatoes made?
Yes, by the provincial government, and for that reason we did not make any distribution of potatoes.
Where were the potatoes obtained?

Pretty much from western Canada, although some were obtained as far east as Fort William, some from the newer part of western Ontario, also from Manitoba, and, I assume, from Alberta and British Columbia.
There were a great many potatoes sent out there from New Brunswick, and I was wondering if any were purchased from New Brunswick.

We did not make these purchases. I would not be absolutely certain, but I do not think they went as far east ns New Brunswick to purchase potatoes. I

think there were sufficient supplies in Manitoba and closer to the area, and therefore there would not be so much freight to pay on them.

I am not complaining at all of the distribution because I think it was a splendid thing and the right thing to do. It not only gave relief to those in Saskatchewan who needed it, but made it possible to help those in eastern Canada who had fruits and vegetables for sale. What I was complaining of particularly was that in the distribution certain people did get fruit and vegetables who did not need them, and the consequence was that those who could have done with a little more did not get it. I have before me a letter which states that the distribution in this particular locality was three-fifths of a box of apples to each person, fifteen pounds of carrots and fourteen pounds of cabbage. It says nothing about potatoes. If that was the only distribution, it would not be a very large quantity of apples for the individual, and the distribution would be less because of people getting these supplies who did not need them. The minister admits, I suppose, having approved that system of distribution, because the letter from Doctor Stapleford says that it is the special request of the minister that everyone should participate and the populations of the municipality and of the urban centres within the municipality are given to make sure that the supplies could be divided accordingly, so that each one would share in them. When the minister is replying he might also give us the parties from whom they collected the beans and also I he fish.
I just gave information about the fish and the beans.

I had reference to the
cheese.

I do not think it has been sent to us yet, but we have a complete list of all the people who got these supplies. When we sent out the supplies we arranged with every person who obtained the apples, when the apples were shipped first, to sign an application for them, to state the number of persons in each family, and to sign for the amount they obtained. The last report that I had before the office was closed up was that they had returns from every municipality regarding the apples, with one exception, and they expected to have that one in within a few days, before the office was closed. I have not inquired since if that one report was in, but the others are. It was intended that there

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
should be a full sign-up on all the other commodities in addition to the apples. They got the list of persons to whom they supplied the fish, beans, cheese and other commodities from the first list of apples shipped. The apples had to be shipped before frost. We got a complete list, and knew from that list what to ship into each municipality to supply individuals. The letter which was sent out, and which, as indicated by the faon. member for Qu'Appelle, was of a general nature, went to rural municipalities. But the instructions which went to the urban centres, that is the villages and towns within the area, indicated that not more than seventy-five per cent of the population was to be supplied. It was indicated clearly at that time that those who were to be left out were persons who were on salaries and were getting along about as well as if tihe drought had not existed, because they were being paid practically the same salaries as before. It was ordered that those people were to be left out of the distribution, and I am quite sure that the instruction was carried out over the greater part of the area, because I had quite a number of letters from different places complaining that it had been carried out.
The statement as issued under date of March 10 to the department at Ottawa contains this sentence.
In answer to question twelve, the goods were distributed not only to those on relief but also to practically all farmers, on the basis that many who were not on relief were suffering even more than those who had accepted relief. To the smaller towns and villages supplies were sent on the basis of seventy-five per cent of the population; that is, it was assumed that in the towns and villages twenty-five per cent of the people would not require the supplies.
That is the answer, I think, which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle himself received on the list of questions given.

Has the minister any
record of the enormous quantities which were given besides those to which he has referred? Added up together from the various parts of Canada, there must have been an enormous number of carloads of gifts, in the form of food as well as clothing, that went in for distribution through the area.
We had complete statements made up. I am speaking from memory when I say that I think the number that was shipped voluntarily this year was about 1,200 cars.
The minister might explain why these cars were all billed to Regina.- Is that the centre from which the carload lots were distributed?

The fish, cheese and
beans?
Well, were not the vegetables shipped there and then transhipped again, rebilled?

The apples were shipped directly to the point and unloaded there. Of course, they had to move cars from one point to another; there might be a car and a half required at one particular point, and then a half car would go on to the next point. Vegetables were handled in very much the same way. The fruit and vegetables had to be got out before the frost, and were distributed to the local points. In so far as cheese, beans and fish were concerned, it was seldom that a carload of any one of them was required at any one point. Those were shipped to Regina, unloaded and repacked in cars in the quantities required at each point, then reshipped to that point and distributed there.

The idea I had was that
when there were fifty-three carloads of cheese and 101 carloads of fish, they might have been shipped, or some of them, directly to points like Weyburn and Swift Current and there distributed, instead of being unloaded at Regina and reshipped or parcelled. Some of the cheese, I understand, was cut into smaller parcels at Regina. I thought they might have had some system of billing in transit like they have for flour, and so on. Possibly that would have saved freight because local freight would be charged from Regina to other points. A great deal of it could have been shipped to and handled at the larger centres like Weyburn and Swift Current.

This was all inquired
into at the time. The man we had in charge was a gentleman who had previously been in charge of Simpson's mail order business. We secured the assistance, by loan from the Canadian National Railways, of a freight man, and from the Canadian Pacific Railway, of another freight man.
And special freight rates.

Yes. These officials
took charge of the whole administration and distribution. I think it is generally admitted that a very good job was made of the distribution itself.
